questions.q: In a conditional type T extends U ? X : Y, what does the extends test ask?
questions.explain: The test is assignability, the same check as const u: U = someT. It is not equality: "NGN" extends string is true, but string extends "NGN" is false.
options: Whether T and U are exactly the same type
Whether every value of T is also a value of U (assignability)
Whether T is a class that inherits from U
Whether U has at least the properties of T

questions.q: What is HasBalance<{ id: string; balanceKobo: number; frozen: boolean }>?
questions.explain: Object types are compared by shape. Extra properties never make a type fail an extends test; the type only has to have a balanceKobo that is a number.
questions.code: type HasBalance<T> = T extends { balanceKobo: number } ? "yes" : "no";

questions.q: What is HasBalance<{ balanceKobo?: number }> with the same HasBalance?
questions.explain: An optional property might be missing, so a value of that type is not guaranteed to have a balanceKobo. It is not assignable to a type that requires one.
questions.code: type HasBalance<T> = T extends { balanceKobo: number } ? "yes" : "no";

questions.q: What is IsText<any>?
questions.explain: any might pass the test and might fail it, so TypeScript returns the union of both branches. One stray any quietly widens every conditional type it reaches.
questions.code: type IsText<T> = T extends string ? "text" : "not text";

questions.q: What is IsText<unknown>?
questions.explain: unknown is not a union and not any. It could be anything, so it is not assignable to string: the false branch.
questions.code: type IsText<T> = T extends string ? "text" : "not text";

questions.q: What is IsText<never>?
questions.explain: T is a naked type parameter, so the type distributes over unions. never is the empty union: zero members, zero evaluations, and the union of zero results is never.
questions.code: type IsText<T> = T extends string ? "text" : "not text";

questions.q: What is IsApproved<boolean>?
questions.explain: boolean is the union true | false. The conditional type distributes: true gives "approved", false gives "pending".
questions.code: type IsApproved<T> = T extends true ? "approved" : "pending";

questions.q: What is ToList<string | number>?
questions.explain: The naked T distributes: string becomes string[], number becomes number[], and the results are unioned. A value is either a list of strings or a list of numbers, never a mix.
questions.code: type ToList<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;

questions.q: Which version gives (string | number)[] for string | number?
questions.explain: Distribution only happens when the checked type is a naked type parameter. Wrapping it in a one-element tuple, [T], asks one question about the whole union.
options: type L<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;
type L<T> = T extends T ? T[] : never;
type L<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;

questions.q: What is MyExclude<"pending" | "paid" | "refunded", "refunded" | "disputed">?
questions.explain: It runs once per member of T. "refunded" matches and becomes never, which disappears from the union. "disputed" is in U but not in T, so it never appears.
questions.code: type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;
options: never, because the whole union does not extend U

questions.q: Which type correctly answers true for never and false for string?
questions.explain: The first one distributes over zero members and gives never. The third is true for every type, because never is assignable to everything. Only the tuple form asks the question once.
options: type IsNever<T> = T extends never ? true : false;
type IsNever<T> = never extends T ? true : false;
type IsNever<T> = T extends unknown ? false : true;

questions.q: What is Direct?
questions.explain: Distribution only happens when a generic type parameter is instantiated with a union. Here the union is written directly, so the whole union is tested once, and 42 is not a string.
questions.code: type Direct = "NGN" | 42 extends string ? true : false;

questions.q: What is ResultOf<typeof refund>?
questions.explain: infer R captures the declared return type as it is, promise included. That is how the built-in ReturnType works; add Awaited to get boolean.

questions.q: Why does ResultOf constrain with (...args: never[]) => … instead of (...args: unknown[]) => …?
questions.explain: (reference: string) => … is not assignable to (...args: unknown[]) => …: someone could call it with a number. It is assignable to (...args: never[]) => …, because nobody can produce a never to pass. So never[] matches every function.
options: Because parameters are checked in the opposite direction: a function that needs a string cannot accept any unknown, but every parameter type accepts never
Because unknown[] is not allowed in a rest parameter

questions.q: What is CurrencyFirst<[1_500_000, "NGN"]>?
questions.explain: infer C extends string only matches when the captured part is a string. The first element is a number, so the pattern fails and the false branch, never, is taken.
questions.code: type CurrencyFirst<T> = T extends readonly [infer C extends string, ...unknown[]] ? C : never;

questions.q: What is Fields<{ success: "paid"; failure: 402 }>?
questions.explain: The same infer name found two candidates in ordinary (output) positions, so TypeScript combines them with a union. In parameter positions it would use an intersection.
questions.code: type Fields<T> = T extends { success: infer V; failure: infer V } ? V : never;

questions.q: What is Unwrap<Promise<Promise<User>> | undefined>?
questions.explain: It distributes over the union. The promise member is unwrapped twice by recursion until the base case, User. undefined does not match the pattern and is returned unchanged.
questions.code: type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? Unwrap<V> : T;

questions.q: Why does real code use the built-in Awaited<T> instead of T extends Promise<infer V> ? Unwrap<V> : T?
questions.explain: Unwrap<PromiseLike<User>> stays PromiseLike<User>, but await would give a User. Awaited handles thenables and is maintained and tested by the TypeScript team.
options: Because await works on any thenable (an object with a then method), and Awaited models that, while matching Promise only knows the real Promise class
Because Unwrap does not distribute over unions

questions.q: A recursive type fails with TS2589 "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite". What is the best first move?
questions.explain: There is no tsconfig option for the limit. Tail-position recursion lets the compiler evaluate about a thousand steps; anything more means the type is doing work that belongs in runtime code, or it never terminates.
options: Check whether the recursion can end, keep the recursive call in tail position, and make the input smaller
Raise TypeScript's recursion limit in tsconfig.json

questions.q: What is Kind<Date>?
questions.explain: The first matching branch wins, like if/else if. A Date is an object, so the broad test swallows it. Put the most specific tests first.
questions.code:
type Kind<T> =
  T extends object ? "group"
  : T extends Date ? "date"
  : "other";

questions.q: A form type uses InputKind<T[K]> for each field. For the optional field launchDate?: Date it gives "date" | "unsupported". Why?
questions.explain: An optional property's type includes undefined, and the conditional type handles each member. Use InputKind<NonNullable<T[K]>>.
options: Because optional properties cannot be mapped
Because T[K] is Date | undefined, and the distributive InputKind also evaluates undefined, which matches no branch

questions.q: Why does return "text"; fail to compile inside function label<T extends string | number>(value: T): T extends string ? "text" : "number", even after if (typeof value === "string")?
questions.explain: Inside the function T is still unknown: it could even be the union string | number. The return type stays unresolved, and almost nothing is assignable to it. Use overloads, or one cast in the implementation plus tests.
options: Because typeof does not narrow inside generic functions
Because narrowing the value does not narrow the type parameter T, so the conditional return type is deferred and TypeScript cannot pick a branch
Because conditional types are not allowed as return types

questions.q: When is a conditional return type better than overloads?
questions.explain: Overloads are clearer for a few fixed cases, but a call with a union or an unresolved T matches none of them. A conditional return type follows whatever T is. Neither way checks the implementation against the return type.
options: When there are only two fixed cases
When generic callers must pass their own type parameter through, for example a function that takes a T that may be either case
When the implementation must be fully checked by the compiler

questions.q: Why is type NaiveEqual<A, B> = A extends B ? (B extends A ? true : false) : false a bad equality test?
questions.explain: The naive version distributes over A and gives in to any. The Equal helper built from two generic function types does neither, which is why type tests use it.
options: It is fine; it is what libraries use
It is itself a distributive conditional type, so NaiveEqual<string | number, string> gives boolean, and any gives boolean too
It is too slow to compile

questions.q: What does a // @ts-expect-error line in a type test prove?
questions.explain: It is a test for a rejection. @ts-ignore hides errors silently; @ts-expect-error demands one, so a rule that stops being enforced is noticed.
options: That the next line runs without throwing
That the next line is rejected by the compiler; if a change makes it compile, the directive is unused and tsc fails
That the next line has no type errors
Nothing; it only hides errors, like @ts-ignore

questions.q: A retry wrapper is applied to every method of a payments client. Which method is not safe to retry automatically?
questions.explain: Retrying is safe for idempotent operations, where doing them twice has the same effect as once. A charge that timed out may have succeeded, so a retry can charge the customer twice, unless the processor supports idempotency keys.
options: charge(cardToken, amountKobo), which takes money from a card

questions.q: With Retried<T> from the lesson, what is the type of payments.baseUrl when the client has baseUrl: string?
questions.explain: A string is not a function, so the conditional type takes the false branch and keeps T[K]. The mapped type adds readonly.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A promise resolved with another promise adopts its value, so nesting flattens at runtime. That is why Promise<Promise<T>> is a type that describes no real value, and why Awaited unwraps recursively.

questions.q: await works on thenables too. What does this print?
questions.explain: Any object with a then method is awaited like a promise. The type of value is string because Awaited models thenables. An Unwrap that only matches Promise would get this wrong.
options: TypeError: receipt is not a promise

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The wrapper tries three times, and all three fail because the function only succeeds on the fourth call. It then throws the last error it saw, from attempt 3.

questions.q: This implementation has a bug in one branch, and it compiles. What does it print?
questions.explain: The type says price is a string, but the number branch wraps the result in an array. The as Formatted<T> is a promise the compiler cannot check, so only a test of each branch finds this. price.length is the array's length, 1.

questions.q: A wrapper uses Object.keys to find the methods to wrap. What does this print?
questions.explain: Class methods live on the prototype, not on the instance, so Object.keys only sees the field. A mapped type over keyof LedgerClient would still list balance: the computed type and the runtime disagree unless the code checks.

questions.q: This runtime function has the same order bug as a badly ordered conditional type. What does it print?
questions.explain: A Date is an object, so the first check catches it and the instanceof Date line is never reached. null is excluded from the first check and falls through to "text". Types and code share the rule: most specific test first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each overload describes one case, so one is a string and many is a string[], and the implementation returns exactly that. Amounts are in kobo, so they are divided by 100.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The type guard's result type is computed with Exclude, so open is typed ("pending" | "paid" | "shipped")[]. The runtime check is what actually removes the cancelled orders; the type only describes the result.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Awaiting the outer promise gives an array, and arrays are not unwrapped: its elements are still promises (typeof a promise is "object"). Promise.all waits for them. A type like Settled<T> needs a separate array branch for exactly this reason.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: -? makes every field required, so the object must list all four, and NonNullable keeps the optional checkIn from producing an extra kind. The filter drops only "text".

questions.q: Finish compact. It returns the items that are not null or undefined, typed as NonNullable<T>[]. Use a type guard so no cast is needed. The program should print 2 ada@shop.ng,tunde@shop.ng.
questions.explain: NonNullable<T> is the distributive conditional type T extends null | undefined ? never : T, which here removes null | undefined from string | null | undefined. The guard item is NonNullable<T> tells filter the result type.

questions.q: Finish without(items, removed). It returns the items that are not in removed, typed as Exclude<T, U>[]. The program should print pending,paid,shipped.
questions.explain: The runtime filter does the removing; the guard item is Exclude<T, U> carries the computed type. Widening removed to readonly T[] lets includes accept any T without a cast.

questions.q: Finish withRetry. The returned function calls fn up to attempts times, returns the first successful result, and throws the last error if every attempt fails. The program should print verified PSK_1 after 3 calls.
questions.explain: return await inside try matters: without await, a rejected promise would escape the catch and no retry would happen. The return type Promise<Awaited<R>> is right whether fn is sync or async.

questions.q: Fix the order of the checks in inputKind so that dates give "date", lists of strings give "tags", and other objects give "group". The program should print date tags group number.
questions.explain: Dates and arrays are objects, so the broad object check must come after them. The same rule applies to a chain of conditional types: the first match wins, so the most specific test goes first.

questions.q: Finish wrapAll. It returns a new object with the same keys: every function is replaced by wrap(fn), every other value is copied. The type Wrapped<T> is given. The program should print 22500 https://api.example-payments.ng.
questions.explain: The mapped conditional type decides per property what the result looks like; the loop must build exactly that. value.apply(client, args) keeps this pointing at the original client, in case a method uses it.

questions.q: Finish formatNaira with its conditional return type: a number of kobo becomes one string like ₦1500.50, an array becomes an array of strings. Use a single as Formatted<T> at the end. The program should print ₦1500.50 ₦1.00|₦2.50.
questions.explain: The conditional return type is deferred inside the function, so the implementation needs one assertion. Keep it at a single return and test both branches, because the compiler cannot check that each branch returns the right shape.

questions.q: Finish settle. It awaits a loader that returns a promise of an array of promises, and returns the array of plain values. The program should print INV-001:500000 INV-002:1000000.
questions.explain: await flattens nested promises but not promises inside an array. Promise.all waits for the elements. TypeScript infers T as Invoice by matching Promise<Promise<T>[]>, the same pattern matching infer does.

questions.q: Finish emit so it calls the handler registered for an event with the payload. The type PayloadOf<H> extracts a handler's event type with infer. The program should print paid ORD-7 1500000.
questions.explain: For callers, PayloadOf<Handlers[K]> ties the payload to the event name, so emit("orderPaid", { sku: "X", left: 1 }) does not compile. Inside, K is unresolved and the conditional type is deferred, so calling the looked-up handler needs one cast, the same trade-off as a conditional return type.
